question:
A graph G has five vertices a, b, c, d, e. Its edges are exactly ab, cd, ce, and de. So G is a single edge ab together with a disjoint triangle on c, d, e. Neither G nor any induced subgraph of it contains a cycle on four vertices or a path on four vertices.
Is G a threshold graph? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Threshold graphs are exactly the (2K2,C4,P4)-free graphs.
evidence: Threshold graphs are the (2K2,C4,P4)-free graphs and therefore a subclass of quasi- threshold graphs.

question:
A rooted forest has a tree with root r, where r has child v. Separately, node u has two children, c1 and c2, and c1 has a child g. Node u is moved so that it becomes a child of v. It adopts its former children c1 and c2, and g stays below c1. The quasi-threshold graph induced by the updated forest is then computed.
In this induced quasi-threshold graph, is u adjacent to both r and g? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: In the induced quasi-threshold graph, a moved node u is connected to its new parent v, all of v's ancestors, all adopted children, and all of those children's descendants.
evidence: In the induced quasi-threshold graph, u is then connected to v and all its ancestors as well as to all adopted children and their descendants.

question: In heterogeneous speed scaling, where each processor $P_p$ has its own power exponent $\alpha_p$, job $J_j$ has work $w_j$, release time $r_j$ and deadline $d_j$, and its density is $\delta_j = w_j/(d_j - r_j)$: what lower bound on every job's density guarantees that, in an optimal schedule, the speed $s_{j,p}$ of each job on each processor is at least 1?

question:
For the Maximum Independent Set problem, a researcher proposes a preprocessing step that replaces every vertex of degree at least 3 by a gadget of three new vertices. The step always produces a graph with more vertices than the input. From any optimal independent set of the transformed graph, an optimal independent set of the original graph can be computed in linear time.
Is this preprocessing step a data reduction rule (a reduction) in the sense used for kernelization and branch-and-reduce? (Yes/No)

question:
The original graph is the path $c - a - u - v - w - b - d$. Here $v$ has exactly two non-adjacent neighbors $u$ and $w$. Folding $v$ with $u$ and $w$ removes $v$, $u$ and $w$ and inserts a new vertex $v'$ adjacent to the union of the neighborhoods of $u$ and $w$, namely $a$ and $b$. The reduced graph is the path $c - a - v' - b - d$. A solver finds the maximum independent set $I'=\{c,v',d\}$ of the reduced graph. It then builds a set for the original graph by deleting $v'$ from $I'$ and inserting $u$ and $w$, which gives $\{c,d,u,w\}$.
Is the resulting set $\{c,d,u,w\}$ a maximum independent set of the original graph? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: After a degree-2 vertex fold of $v$ with non-adjacent neighbors $u$ and $w$ into a new vertex $v'$, a maximum independent set $I'$ of the reduced graph is lifted to a maximum independent set of the original graph as $I=(I'\setminus\{v'\})\cup\{u,w\}$ if $v'\in I'$, and otherwise as $I=(I'\setminus\{v'\})\cup\{v\}$.
evidence: If w is in I, one can obtain an independent set of the same size by removing w from I and adding v instead. (2) For the degree-2 vertex fold (see Fig. 2) one removes vertices v with exactly two neighbors u and w that are not adjacent to each other.
In this case a new vertex v′ is inserted and connected to the union of the neighborhoods of u and w yielding a reduction of the graph size by two vertices.
Finally, if v′ is part of an MIS I′ of the reduced graph, then I = (I′ \ {v′}) ∪{u,w} is an MIS of the original graph.
Otherwise, I = (I′ \{v′})∪{v} is an MIS of the original graph.

key_points: At least $\Omega(\log\log n)$ agents are required
question: For deterministic exploration of undirected graphs with $n$ vertices by multiple agents, each agent has only $O(\log^{1-\varepsilon} n)$ bits of memory for some constant $\varepsilon>0$. What lower bound on the number of agents is known in this setting?
atom_statement: Deterministic exploration of undirected graphs of size $n$ requires at least $\Omega(\log\log n)$ agents if each agent is allowed only $O(\log^{1-\varepsilon} n)$ bits of memory, where $\varepsilon>0$.

question:
A developer implements a suffix array construction routine for a string $T$ of length 1,000,000 over a byte alphabet. The routine first picks out only the suffixes starting at positions divisible by 3 (positions 0, 3, 6, ...). It forms a new string in which each block of three consecutive characters is a single character, and it recurses on this string until all characters are unique. From the resulting order it derives the order of the suffixes starting at positions not divisible by 3, and finally merges the two sorted lists into the full suffix array.
Is this routine an instance of the DC3 (difference-cover modulo 3) suffix array construction algorithm? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The DC3 difference-cover algorithm first computes $SA_{12}$ for the suffixes starting at positions not divisible by 3. It does this by treating three characters as one and recursing until all characters are unique. It then computes $SA_0$ of the remaining suffixes using $SA_{12}$ and merges $SA_0$ and $SA_{12}$ into the final SA.
evidence: First, we compute SA12 containing all sufﬁxes starting at positions that are not a multiple of three, i.e., sufﬁxes starting at positions that are congruent to 1 and 2 modulo 3.
To this end, we interpret three characters as one (increasing the alphabet size) and recursively call this algorithm until all characters are unique.
Then, the SA0 of all other sufﬁxes is computed using the already computed SA12.
To obtain the ﬁnal SA, SA0 and SA12 are merged.

question:
A developer writes a generator that adds nodes one at a time. For each new node, it must pick $m$ distinct existing nodes as neighbors, where each existing node is chosen with probability proportional to its current degree. After every inserted edge, the degrees of the chosen nodes change, so the selection weights are different for the next node. The graph has several billion edges.
Is this neighbor-selection step, drawing from weights that keep changing, the main algorithmic challenge in generating Barabási–Albert (BA) graphs? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The main algorithmic challenge of generating BA graphs is the dynamic weighted sampling of neighbors.
evidence: The main algorithmic challenge of BA lies in this dynamic weighted sampling.

question:
An external-memory BA generator stores its edge list on disk, and the graph is far larger than main memory. For each edge it needs to know which earlier position of the edge list to copy from. The generator does not look up these positions one at a time. It first produces the complete list of positions that will be needed, without reading anything, and sorts that list by position. It then makes a single sequential pass over the edge list to fetch the values.
Does this generator use the read strategy of TFP-BA, in which the required reads are precomputed and sorted by the memory address they read from instead of being issued at random positions? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Instead of reading from random positions in the edge list, TFP-BA first precomputes all necessary read operations and sorts them by the memory address they read from.
evidence: Rather than reading from random positions in the edge list, TFP-BA ﬁrst pre- computes all necessary read operations and sorts them by the memory address they read from.

question:
A practitioner has the problem $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^2} \|x\|_1 = |x_1|+|x_2|$ subject to the equality constraint $h(x)=x_1+2x_2-3=0$ and the inequality constraint $g(x)=x_1^2+x_2^2-4\le 0$. The constraint functions $h$ and $g$ are smooth, and both constraints are scalar-valued ($m=1$, $p=1$).
Is this problem within the class of constrained problems for which the augmented Lagrangian method is formulated as a solution approach? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The augmented Lagrangian method is a way to solve constrained problems of the form $\min_x f(x)$ s.t. $h(x)=0$ and $g(x)\le 0$, where $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, $h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ and $g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p$ are differentiable and the constraints are understood component-wise.
